explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is, friend. God says, "…take a brick, place it before you, and draw on it the city of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 4:1) Ezekiel is a prophet, and the first thing he gets is a drawing job. I've stamped a lot of cookies, but nobody ever handed me a brick and said "make it look like a city."

Close, friend, but Babylon isn't the city on the brick. Ezekiel 4:1 says he is to "…draw on it the city of Jerusalem." Ezekiel is living among the exiles by the River Kebar (Ezekiel 1:1), so Babylon might feel like the easy guess. I'd have guessed it too, and I once mixed up my own oven for the cooling rack.

Nineveh is a city the Bible mentions, but it's not the one on this brick. God says, "…draw on it the city of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 4:1) The whole siege that follows is aimed at Jerusalem. Nineveh gets to sit this one out.

True, friend. God says, "Construct a siege wall, build a ramp to it, set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it on all sides." (Ezekiel 4:2) So Ezekiel is building a whole little battle scene. On a brick. I think that's the most detailed work order anybody ever got.

This one is true, friend. Ezekiel 4:2 says, "Construct a siege wall, build a ramp to it, set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it on all sides." The ramp and the camps are both right there in the verse. Easy to second-guess when the whole thing happens on a brick, I get it.

A sign, friend. God says of the siege, "This will be a sign to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 4:3) Ezekiel turns his face toward the city on the brick and besieges it. The iron plate he sets up as an iron wall is part of it too.

Not a gift, friend. God says, "This will be a sign to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 4:3) The city of Jerusalem is drawn on the brick, and the siege works are built against it (Ezekiel 4:1-2). A gift I'd gladly take, but this one is a sign.

Not a test, friend. The verse says, "This will be a sign to the house of Israel." (Ezekiel 4:3) The brick, the iron plate and the turned face are all there to show something. I bet a test would've been easier to ignore, but a sign you can see.

On his right side, friend. God says, "…lie down again, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah." (Ezekiel 4:6) First it was the left side for the house of Israel, now the right side for Judah. Ezekiel is getting a full rotation, and I think he'd have paid good money for a pillow.

Flat on his back sounds comfy, friend, but that's not the instruction. God says, "…lie down again, but on your right side…" (Ezekiel 4:6) The first stretch was on his left side (Ezekiel 4:4), so this time it's the other side.

Not facedown, friend. The verse says, "…lie down again, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah." (Ezekiel 4:6) I dive face-first into my chocolate chips on purpose, but that's just me. Ezekiel's job is a side-lying job.

Careful with this one, friend, because it's false. God says, "I have assigned to you 40 days, a day for each year." (Ezekiel 4:6) Each day stands for one year, not one week. The same goes for the 390 days on his left side (Ezekiel 4:5).

False is right, friend. God says, "I have assigned to you 40 days, a day for each year." (Ezekiel 4:6) So each day stands for a year, not a week. The same pattern works for the 390 days on the left side (Ezekiel 4:5).

Prophesy against it, friend. God says, "You must turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against it." (Ezekiel 4:7) The bared arm and the steady face go with the words he speaks. Ezekiel gets the whole message across, and I'd say that's a pretty full-body sermon.

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "…turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against it." (Ezekiel 4:7) The job is to prophesy against it. Praying is a good thing to do, but it's not what this verse tells Ezekiel to do.

No singing here, friend. God says Ezekiel is to "…prophesy against it." (Ezekiel 4:7) His face is turned toward the siege and his arm is bared. I'd love a musical number, but this passage doesn't have one.

Ropes, friend. God says, "Now behold, I will tie you up with ropes so you cannot turn from side to side until you have finished the days of your siege." (Ezekiel 4:8) So Ezekiel isn't left to flip over on his own. I think that takes the snooze-button temptation right out.

Iron shows up in this passage, but not on Ezekiel. God says, "…I will tie you up with ropes…" (Ezekiel 4:8) The iron is the plate set up as a wall in Ezekiel 4:3. The ropes are what hold him in place.

No guard in this passage, friend. God says, "…I will tie you up with ropes so you cannot turn from side to side…" (Ezekiel 4:8) The ropes do the job. A guard would just be one more person standing around watching him lie there.

A single container, friend. God says, "put them in a single container and make them into bread for yourself." (Ezekiel 4:9) Wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt all go in together. In my bakery I keep my toppings in separate bowls, so this would give me a twitch.

Six jars would be tidy, friend, but that's not what God says. The verse says, "put them in a single container and make them into bread for yourself." (Ezekiel 4:9) All six ingredients go into one. Separate jars would be great for my sprinkles, but not for this bread.
Two pots, friend? The verse says one: "put them in a single container…" (Ezekiel 4:9) All six ingredients go in together and become the bread. Two pots would be one pot too many.

This one is false, friend. God says, "You are to weigh out twenty shekels of food to eat each day, and you are to eat it at set times." (Ezekiel 4:10) So Ezekiel doesn't get to graze whenever his stomach complains. That's one strict schedule.
False is right, friend. God says, "…you are to eat it at set times." (Ezekiel 4:10) The amount is weighed out and the timing is set too. That's a strict schedule, and I'd be in trouble with it.

explanations.answer: In the nations He will banish them to
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. The LORD says, "This is how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I will banish them." (Ezekiel 4:13) So the bread Ezekiel eats is a picture of how the Israelites will eat. It's a heavy picture, and the verse doesn't dress it up.

explanations.answer: In the courts of His holy temple
explanations.explanation: Not the temple courts, friend. The verse says the Israelites will eat their defiled bread "…among the nations to which I will banish them." (Ezekiel 4:13) The place is among the nations. That's far from home.

explanations.answer: In the wilderness of Mount Sinai
explanations.explanation: Not Sinai, friend. The LORD says, "…among the nations to which I will banish them." (Ezekiel 4:13) Sinai is the mountain in Exodus 19, a different story altogether. Here the bread gets eaten among the nations.

True, friend. Ezekiel says, "Ah, Lord GOD, I have never defiled myself." (Ezekiel 4:14) He goes on to say that from his youth until now he hasn't eaten anything found dead or mauled by wild beasts, and no unclean meat has entered his mouth. He speaks up plainly, and I respect that.

It's true, friend. Ezekiel says to God, "I have never defiled myself." (Ezekiel 4:14) He adds that from his youth until now he hasn't eaten anything found dead or mauled by wild beasts. That's him speaking up, not keeping quiet.

explanations.answer: What he bakes his bread over
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. God replies, "I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that." (Ezekiel 4:15) So the fuel changes, and everything else stays. Ezekiel spoke up and God answered him, and I think that's worth noticing.

explanations.answer: How many days he lies down
explanations.explanation: The days stay the same, friend. What God changes is this: "I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that." (Ezekiel 4:15) The 390 days and the 40 days aren't touched. Only the baking fuel changes.

explanations.answer: Which grains go in his bread
explanations.explanation: The grains stay put, friend. God's reply is, "I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that." (Ezekiel 4:15) So the change is about what he bakes over. The wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt are still on the list.

Weight, friend. God says, "They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight…" (Ezekiel 4:16) That matches Ezekiel's own food, which he weighs out each day (Ezekiel 4:10). In Jerusalem it comes with anxiety, and I think that's a hard way to eat.

Not family, friend. The verse says, "They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight…" (Ezekiel 4:16) The bread is rationed by weight. Ezekiel has already been weighing out his food, so the word is a familiar one (Ezekiel 4:10).

Not tribe, friend. God says, "They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight…" (Ezekiel 4:16) The word is weight, like the twenty shekels of food Ezekiel weighs out each day (Ezekiel 4:10). Weight is the word the verse gives.

Iniquity, friend. God says, "they will be appalled at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity." (Ezekiel 4:17) The same word has been all through this passage, like when Ezekiel bears the iniquity of the house of Israel (Ezekiel 4:4-5). It's a heavy ending.

Pride isn't the word, friend. The verse says they will be appalled "…at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity." (Ezekiel 4:17) Iniquity is the word that keeps coming back in this passage (Ezekiel 4:4-6). It's a heavy verse.

Not anger, friend. God says they will be appalled "…at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity." (Ezekiel 4:17) The word iniquity shows up earlier too, when Ezekiel bears it on his side (Ezekiel 4:5-6). That's a heavy word.
